    #3595. What Ron Johnson's 'Ponzi scheme' label gets wrong about Social Security, experts say

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1279 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    What Ron Johnson's 'Ponzi scheme' label gets wrong about Social Security, experts say

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1279 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A newly introduced Senate budget committee hearing on Wednesday reignited an old Social Security question: Is the program, which provides monthly benefits to millions of Americans, a Ponzi scheme?
    • Industry observers note that senate Budget Committee Chairman Ron Johnson, a Republican representing Wisconsin, called Social Security "a legal Ponzi scheme" in his opening remarks.
    • A Ponzi scheme is an investment fraud that uses funds from new investors to pay existing investors, according to the Securities and Exchange Commission, Johnson wrote in his chairman's hearing memo.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A newly introduced Senate budget committee hearing on Wednesday reignited an old Social Security question: Is the program, which provides monthly benefits to millions of Americans, a Ponzi scheme?

    Industry observers note that senate Budget Committee Chairman Ron Johnson, a Republican representing Wisconsin, called Social Security "a legal Ponzi scheme" in his opening remarks. But experts say his comments overlook how Social Security works and the real dilemma for lawmakers over its looming funding shortfall.

    A Ponzi scheme is an investment fraud that uses funds from new investors to pay existing investors, according to the Securities and Exchange Commission, Johnson wrote in his chairman's hearing memo. He said that Social Security fits the description if you remove the word "fraud.".

    Johnson's comments followed his Wednesday morning interview on Fox Business, where he said, "At this point, there's really no way to fix Social Security.".

    "You can't fix it, you just shut it down and then hope that you can recover some of your money," Johnson noted during the Fox Business interview.

    It has been revealed that "As far as I can tell, this is the first time in decades that a senior senator, chairman of the budget committee, said he would rather shut down Social Security than fix it," Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., said during the hearing.

    At the Senate hearing, Johnson said his comments during the TV interview were "imprecise" and that he was talking broadly about Ponzi schemes, not Social Security, that need to be shut down.

    Johnson noted he wants lawmakers to pass a law to ensure seniors' Social Security benefits are not reduced, "then roll up our sleeves and fix the real problem, which is $24 trillion of 10-year deficits.".

    The Congressional Budget Office has projected a $24.4 trillion cumulative federal budget deficit over the next 10 years.

    Johnson proposed a bill on Wednesday that would allow for Social Security retirement benefits to be funded by general revenue once that trust fund reaches its insolvency date.

    Critics say that's not a viable solution. Using the general fund to pay for Social Security would "absolutely explode the national debt" and cost 165% of gross domestic product over 75 years, Maya MacGuineas, president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a nonpartisan organization, remarked in a statement.

    The way Johnson described the program during the hearing was "out of touch with the way the American public understands and knows Social Security," said Bill Sweeney, senior vice president of government affairs at AARP, a nonprofit, nonpartisan organization representing Americans age 50 and over.

    It has been revealed that "The budget committee should know that Social Security is not part of the budget," Sweeney remarked. "It runs on its own budget.".

    Social Security does affect the unified federal deficit and debt held by the public when outlays exceed dedicated revenues, according to CBO. The Treasury securities held by Social Security's trust funds count as intragovernmental debt, which is included in gross federal debt but not in debt held by the public.

    According to recent reports, social Security benefits are mainly funded by payroll tax contributions. When the program's income exceeds its costs, the surplus is invested in special U.S. Treasury securities held in the trust funds.

    Social Security is not allowed to borrow money and cannot go into debt, according to Sweeney.

    Sources indicate that "It's never contributed a penny to the debt," Sweeney mentioned. "It's not part of the national debt because it's in a separate budget.".

    Recent findings suggest that social Security's trust funds may be depleted within the next six to eight years, based on current projections. If that happens, Social Security benefits may be cut.

    Recent findings suggest that in six years — the fourth quarter of 2032 — the Social Security retirement trust fund may run out, Social Security's trustees projected in June. At that time, 78% of those benefits would be payable.

    In eight years — the third quarter of 2034 — Social Security's combined retirement and disability trust funds may run out, when 83% of scheduled benefits would be payable, according to the Social Security trustees' projections.

    Had payroll tax revenue kept up with gross domestic product over the past four decades, the program would be able to pay full benefits until 2059 — an additional 25 years versus current projections, according to recent AARP research.

    At the hearing, Johnson held up a picture of the trust funds, which he remarked is a "four-drawer file in Parkersburg, West Virginia.".

    In a recent development, johnson similarly mentioned the trust fund files at a July 2023 hearing. In 2005, then-President George W. Bush was shown paper evidence of Social Security's U.S. bonds during a visit to the Bureau of Public Debt in Parkersburg.

    While the politicians' actions seem to suggest the trust funds aren't real, experts say they are legitimate.

    "It's all about trying to scare people into thinking that Social Security is not going to be there for you when it's time for you to retire," Sweeney noted. "For 91 years it has been, and there's no reason to believe it won't be.".

    Wednesday's Senate hearing was a "missed opportunity" for a more in-depth discussion of the challenges facing Social Security, mentioned Jason Fichtner, a witness at the hearing and executive director of the LIMRA Retirement Income Institute, a research initiative within the insurance trade association LIMRA.

    Aims such as raising or eliminating the taxable maximum for payroll contributions to Social Security may push the program's funding woes 20 or 30 years later, but would not make the program solvent for the 75-year target, according to Fichtner, a former Social Security Administration official.

    Moreover, fixing Social Security would not resolve the government's larger fiscal issues, which would still leave the economy vulnerable to bond market strain, he said.

    "The other glitch is fear," Fichtner remarked. "We do see evidence now of people claiming Social Security earlier because of their fear of the trust funds running out of money or Social Security not being able to pay benefits.".

    A June 2025 AARP survey found 49% of respondents who had recently claimed or planned to claim Social Security benefits earlier than planned were mostly motivated by concerns the program may run out of money.

    "Social Security is very effective at solving problems, and it's a thorn in the side of the federal government because they have done a horrible job managing so many aspects of our finances," said labor economist Kathryn Anne Edwards, a witness at the hearing and a senior fellow at the National Academy of Social Insurance, a provider of research and policy analysis on social insurance and economic security programs.

    "But Americans don't see it that way," she said.

    More than half of Social Security recipients surveyed say benefits are their main source of income, according to an August AARP poll.

    According to recent reports, social Security reform provides an opportunity to expand the program to help meet Americans' needs, Edwards mentioned. Adding universal paid family and medical leave to the program could help individuals and families who don't at the moment have access to those benefits, she said. Moreover, strengthening unemployment insurance could help ensure financial security amid the prospect of AI-related job losses, Edwards said.

    Senators who were elected on Nov. 3 will be in office when the retirement trust fund depletion date hits in 2032. The next session of Congress may provide an opportunity for "serious" hearings on the future of Social Security, Sweeney said.

    The Senate budget committee's Wednesday hearing followed other recent hearings on the program's future, including a June Senate finance subcommittee hearing and an August Senate finance full committee hearing.

    #3592. Junk bonds are 'flashing yellow.' Watch these warning signs

    📅 09 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1026 w)
    📖 Baca
    Gadgets ⚠️ Warning 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Junk bonds are 'flashing yellow.' Watch these warning signs

    📅 09 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1026 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that cracks are forming in the junk bond market as investors demand higher payouts for owning the market's riskiest debt.
    • According to recent reports, high-yield bonds now yield 8.1%, up from 7.22% a month ago.
    • The high-yield market is also showing stress on the credit side with spreads recently widening to levels not seen since April, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that cracks are forming in the junk bond market as investors demand higher payouts for owning the market's riskiest debt. It isn't time to ditch high-yield bonds, but investors should pay attention to the warning signs.

    According to recent reports, high-yield bonds now yield 8.1%, up from 7.22% a month ago. The increase reflects a jump in yields across the curve as investors bake in more inflation from high energy prices and other pressures, including concern about the deficit — hitting nearly $2 trillion in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30.

    The high-yield market is also showing stress on the credit side with spreads recently widening to levels not seen since April, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Credit spreads are the difference in yield between the bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. Wider spreads mean investors are demanding higher yields for holding corporate debt, viewing it as riskier.

    Spreads are at 315 basis points in the overall high-yield market, higher than a year ago but still below levels in March when they reached 346 bps. One basis point equals one one-hundredth of a percent, or 0.01%.

    The high-yield market consists of bonds rated BB+ by S&P and Fitch and Ba1 and under by Moody's. The lowest-rated cohort, CCC and below, has seen the most movement with spreads climbing dramatically over the past year to roughly 1,250 bps.

    Right now, the high-yield market is "flashing yellow" but is "far from red," said Michael Arone, chief investment strategist at State Street Investment Management.

    It makes sense that investors are demanding more compensation for taking on additional credit risk as borrowing costs rise, he noted.

    Yields are elevated across the board with the 10-year Treasury reaching its highest level since 2002 earlier in the week.

    "The bigger question is whether this is simply a repricing of interest rate risk, or the beginning of a more fundamental reassessment of credit quality," Arone said.

    He's in a wait-and-see mode since earnings are still growing, interest-coverage ratios remain good, and while default rates have ticked up some, he believes it is not concerning.

    That said, the starting point in spreads is likely weighing on investors' psyche, since they are still low by historical standards.

    "There's a small margin of error here, which I also think raises the anxiety level," Arone explained. "The compensation that investors are receiving for taking on this credit risk isn't overwhelming relative to history, and therefore subtle changes in credit spreads can be concerning.".

    While there may be concerns about part of the lower-rated market, the overall high-yield market is in good fundamental shape.

    In fact, credit quality is at a record high, with BB bonds making up over 60% of the market compared with 38% prior to the global financial crisis, mentioned Kelley Gerrity, a fixed income strategist at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.

    "We've had higher-quality companies coming in, and with higher rates now, you also have more discipline from companies that are more indebted ... just because of the higher cost of capital, so that actually is creating a bit of a healthier picture as well," she said.

    The lowest tier of high yield has always been more speculative, since the bonds have a higher default risk. Therefore, it's no surprise that they are the ones seeing the most widening in spreads, remarked Collin Martin, head of fixed income research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research.

    Sources indicate that the overall move in high-yield spreads have been "orderly," he said. "Are there cracks forming? I think the cracks are logical cracks with the lowest-rated bonds and it's too early to say that it's spreading to the broad credit market.".

    It has been revealed that in addition, fluctuations within the CCC-rated and lower spreads have been idiosyncratic, Gerrity added. Morgan Stanley recently broke down the spreads in the lowest cohort into two buckets: performing assets and non-performing assets, which are defined as spreads above 1,000 bps.

    The non-performing spread to worst is 2,818 bps, while the performing bucket — the biggest piece of the CCC market — is 461 bps, she remarked.

    "It is isolated," she mentioned. "I'm not necessarily sure that that will go away anytime soon, but it doesn't tell the story of overall concern and flashing caution for credit markets right now.".

    For now, investors should remain selective within higher yield, Gerrity advised.

    "We're looking for the best relative value opportunities, and we think that exists within that single-B cohort, and so we're leaning into that," she stated.

    Investors should be concerned if there is a steep widening in the broader high-yield market.

    But there's scant evidence of stress in the BB cohort. Spreads in that group are at 194 bps, up from 179 bps a year ago — although the move hasn't been in a straight line.

    Industry observers note that "We're going to be focusing our attention on what are considered some stronger businesses," Martin said. "If we start to see the markets demand higher spreads there also, that's what we'll be looking at to see if risks are really rising.".

    Industry observers note that it's also crucial to understand that the Federal Reserve is raising rates in a strong economic environment, remarked R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. The central bank is concerned about an inflation problem amid high fossil fuel prices due to the Iran war, while growth has been stronger than expected, he noted.

    "With growth being good as the reason that the Fed is hiking, then you wouldn't expect high yield to blow out because growth means revenues stay up, means cash flow and profitability stays up," he explained.

    High yield becomes a disaster when the economy is heading into a sharp economic downturn, Gallo stated.

    Recent findings suggest that "That's when spreads really widen out," he said. "But a recession is not the odds-on bet. Now, talk to me in six months if the Fed keeps hiking over and over, if oil prices stay high for longer, well, then maybe we will start to wonder.".

    Netflix, Amazon, Fox to bid for 2030 men's World Cup rights; Disney out

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (542 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Netflix, Amazon, YouTube and Fox are all expected to submit offers to win the U.S.
    • It has been revealed that fox and NBCU's Telemundo are the incumbent rights holders.
    • CNBC previously reported that media executives are planning on the winning bid coming in around $1.5 billion — or maybe even higher — although that amount could vary somewhat depending on whether both 2030 and 2034 are acquired.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Netflix, Amazon, YouTube and Fox are all expected to submit offers to win the U.S. media rights for the 2030 men's World Cup before today's deadline, according to people familiar with the matter — but Disney will not be putting in a bid.

    It has been revealed that fox and NBCU's Telemundo are the incumbent rights holders. FIFA would prefer to sell both the English and Spanish rights together, to one buyer, for the 2030 World Cup, to be held in Spain, Portugal and Morocco. Media companies also have the right to bid on the 2034 World Cup, which will be held in Saudi Arabia.

    CNBC previously reported that media executives are planning on the winning bid coming in around $1.5 billion — or maybe even higher — although that amount could vary somewhat depending on whether both 2030 and 2034 are acquired.

    FIFA is open to the idea of a potential partnership bid in which rights are split between a traditional broadcaster and a streamer, to maximize reach. Still, unlike in other countries where there are government mandates on airing games for free, FIFA will not mandate that a subscription streamer sublicense games. That decision will be up to the winning bidder.

    According to recent reports, FIFA is satisfied that enough people in the U.S. already have a Netflix or Amazon Prime Video subscription that reach won't be an glitch, according to people familiar with the matter. The 2027 Women's World Cup will be on Netflix in the U.S., and Netflix intends to air all of the games without a partner.

    Disney/ESPN will not be bidding, according to people familiar with the matter. ESPN Chairman Jimmy Pitaro mentioned he was interested in World Cup rights earlier this year at CNBC Sport x Boardroom's Game Initiative Summit.

    It has been revealed that in recent weeks, ESPN ran the numbers and couldn't get to $1.5 billion or higher while also having to save money for NHL, MLB and European soccer — English Premier League and Champions League — all of which will likely renew their media rights deals in 2027, noted the people, who asked not to be named because the discussions were private. ESPN looked into entering a bid with a partner but ultimately decided not to bid, one of the people said.

    Industry observers note that NBCUniversal still hasn't made a decision on bidding, potentially putting Telemundo in jeopardy of losing the games for 2030, according to a person familiar with the matter. NBCUniversal has already spent billions on NBA and also needs to save money for both MLB and EPL potentially as well as the NFL, which will likely be a 2028 negotiation.

    Skydance and Apple will not bid, according to people familiar with the matter.

    A FIFA spokesperson declined to comment, citing confidentiality of the tender process.

    Recent findings suggest that FIFA executives blueprint to travel to the U.S. next week to meet personally with bidders to assess their bids and potentially get final offers. FIFA plans to choose a winner before the end of the year.

    #3582. As Sanofi's Pompe drug shortage drags on, some patients struggle to access treatments

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (917 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    As Sanofi's Pompe drug shortage drags on, some patients struggle to access treatments

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (917 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Two weeks ago, Monique Griffin got a troubling email.
    • The French drugmaker Sanofi told her that a shipping delay had interrupted supply of the drug that she relies on to manage her rare muscle-wasting disease.
    • In a recent development, "You're basically letting the disease take over again," she said.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Two weeks ago, Monique Griffin got a troubling email.

    The French drugmaker Sanofi told her that a shipping delay had interrupted supply of the drug that she relies on to manage her rare muscle-wasting disease. Her next infusion was canceled. Griffin, who is 51 and uses a wheelchair due to Pompe disease, fears what will happen if the shortage isn't resolved soon.

    In a recent development, "You're basically letting the disease take over again," she said. "It's terrifying.".

    Industry observers note that more than three months after initial reports of supply problems with treatments for Pompe disease, the disruption drags on, with more patients learning their infusions have been canceled. Sanofi remarked it has made progress restoring the supply to patients in some countries, but added that shipping delays could interrupt infusions for some U.S. patients through the end of November.

    A Sanofi spokesperson said there were no issues with drug quality and the organization is "committed to ensuring that the most vulnerable patients receive treatment first during this period." The company added that patients should speak with a health professional before taking another treatment, adding, "these medicines are not interchangeable.".

    In a statement, the Food and Drug Administration said "patient access to these treatments is a priority for the agency and we have offered our assistance to Sanofi on anything needed to help ensure all patient needs are met.".

    About one in every 19,000 babies is born with Pompe disease, which is named after the Dutch pathologist who discovered the condition nearly a century ago.

    Patients lack an enzyme for breaking down a complex sugar, causing a toxic buildup of glycogen inside their cells. Their muscles weaken and their heart can become enlarged. They have trouble breathing and eating. Left untreated, the disease is often fatal.

    According to recent reports, sanofi's Lumizyme and a second-generation version, Nexviazyme, replace the missing enzyme, protecting the patient's muscles. Patients typically receive Sanofi's drugs every two weeks.

    "It's a lifeline," remarked Jenna Yarborough, a rare disease advocate whose two children with Pompe disease have not been affected by the drug shortage.

    While Pompe disease patients rely on Sanofi's drugs, several other treatments have entered clinical trials, including separate gene therapies from AskBio and Astellas Pharma.

    In a recent development, sanofi says the drug shortage is the result of issues at its manufacturing facility in Ireland, which public documents show the manufacturer has known about for several months. The FDA inspected the plant between January 12 and January 20, 2026 and found violations involving two unrelated drugs. The company began responding to the violations in February, but on June 22, the FDA sent the company a warning letter saying it had still not addressed the "underlying failure" to comply with manufacturing requirements. Addressing the FDA's ongoing concerns has contributed to the supply disruption of the Pompe therapies, according to Sanofi.

    Recent findings suggest that there's a sense of frustration within the Pompe community that the tech giant did not do enough to warn patients about the potential for a supply disruption. Ryan Colburn, a person living with Pompe who is active in the advocacy space, states many patients were unaware of the manufacturing issues at Sanofi and were left with no way to prepare for them. "The lack of proactive transparency and apparent lack of buffer are of huge concern for any medicine that people's lives and well-being depend on access to," Colburn said.

    A spokesperson for Sanofi responded, "As the situation evolved, and the extent of the disruption became clearer, we engaged global and U.S. patient advocacy organizations, patients and clinicians to inform them, and we have worked to continue to keep these groups and individuals updated through regular communications. We remain committed to continuity of care and to transparent, ongoing communication with the Pompe community as we work to stabilize supply.".

    It has been revealed that chelsey McGee's 10-year-old son Logan has taken Lumizyme every two weeks since he was diagnosed with Pompe disease as an infant. While his infusions haven't been canceled yet, she's concerned that missing even one appointment will damage his heart. Sanofi's drug has kept him healthy enough to play soccer.

    "It's important that we stay on his timeline and keep his heart healthy," she remarked.

    Sources indicate that mcGee, who lives in Minneapolis, is frustrated by what she says is a lack of transparency from Sanofi. She discovered the FDA cited the pharmaceutical manufacturer for manufacturing problems by searching the agency's website, not from the company.

    Sources indicate that griffin, who lives in Orlando, has taken Lumizyme since 2010 when she was diagnosed with an adult-onset version of the disease. The diagnosis came after she became so fatigued that she fell while carrying groceries and suffered a concussion.

    She knows what it's like to go without her infusions. She missed a few appointments earlier this year due to an insurance mix-up. She likened it to having "a really bad flu." She became extremely fatigued, struggled to breathe and started to feel pain in her legs, arms and back.

    Pompe is a progressive disease, meaning it gets worse over time. She worries most about losing the strength to breathe. She sleeps with assisted ventilation.

    She works in the theme parks industry and is hoping to attend a conference this week. While her Lumizyme infusions remain on hold, she hopes to get through the week of meetings "on caffeine and goodwill.".

    CNBC Cures is underwritten by Alexion, AstraZeneca Rare Disease and BridgeBio.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Fears around the artificial intelligence trade and higher pressure on oil prices are weighing on global markets, but a few stocks offer investors solid growth prospects even in choppy times.

    Investors with a long-term horizon can look beyond the ongoing volatility and track the recommendations of top Wall Street analysts to pick attractive stocks with strong long-term growth potential.

    Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

    Industry observers note that health insurer UnitedHealth delivered better-than-expected results for the third quarter of 2026. The company also raised its full-year earnings outlook, reflecting continued progress on its turnaround plan.

    Recent findings suggest that following the Q3 print, Morgan Stanley analyst Erin Wright reiterated a buy rating on UNH stock with a price target of $529. "UNH's beat & raise reinforces turnaround momentum, with improving MA [Medicare Advantage]/Optum Health supporting a higher '26 EPS baseline & upside to '27 consensus," remarked Wright.

    The five-star analyst added that better-than-expected performance in the UnitedHealthcare and Optum Health businesses supported another upgrade to the company's 2026 adjusted earnings per share outlook to at least $20.50. Wright noted that UNH raised the earnings guidance despite incremental investments planned for the fourth quarter of 2026.

    Furthermore, Wright highlighted management's view that the consensus 2027 EPS of $22.63 was too conservative. Reaching even the low end of the tech giant's 13% to 16% long-term EPS growth target would imply an EPS of $23.17.

    Wright raised her 2026 EPS estimate to $20.65 from $19.82 and 2027 EPS to $23.24 from $22.54, reflecting the latest upside and an improving 2026 medical loss ratio to 87.4% from 88.1%. Overall, she believes that UNH's operational performance continues to improve, increasing her confidence in its UHC strategy and Optum Health turnaround execution.

    Wright ranks No. 264 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 15%. See UnitedHealth Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

    Sources indicate that social media giant Meta Platforms has been making headlines since the launch of its Muse AI agent, which is seeing solid traction. Investors look forward to updates on the tech giant's AI strategy when it reveals its third-quarter results on Oct. 21.

    Industry observers note that heading into Q3 earnings, Guggenheim analyst Michael Morris maintained a buy rating on Meta stock and increased his price target to $850 from $700, reflecting higher estimates for 2027. He expects Muse usage momentum and engagement levels to shape investor sentiment into the Q3 earnings call.

    Specifically, Morris highlighted that, according to Apptopia, Muse reached 1.3 million daily active users in five weeks versus 300,000 in the first week. Given that Muse's current adoption represents less than 0.05% of Meta's 3.6 billion daily active user base, the analyst expects management to prioritize boosting usage over near-term monetization.

    Recent findings suggest that "Over time, we believe Muse monetizes primarily through businesses paying to reach consumers through their agents, consistent with the economics of Meta's core advertising business, rather than consumer wallets," stated the five-star analyst. He added that the checkout integrations with Shopify and PayPal reflect this framework.

    While there are concerns that a rival could overtake Muse or the recently introduced Muse Wonder and push Meta into a prolonged cycle of overinvestment, Morris remains bullish due to the firm's strong record in scaling WhatsApp and competing strongly with TikTok via Reels as well as free distribution to an extensive user base.

    According to recent reports, morris ranks No. 629 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.2%. See Meta Platforms KPIs on TipRanks.

    Next is semiconductor company Marvell Technology. Earlier this month, Marvell held its Investor Day, where it raised its total addressable market estimate to $400 billion by 2030, reflecting solid AI-led demand tailwinds.

    After hosting a non-deal roadshow with Marvell's senior management following the Investor Day, Stifel analyst Tore Svanberg reiterated a buy rating on the stock with a price target of $370.

    The five-star analyst stated that a major focus of the roadshow was the XPU and XPU Attach mix, as Marvell's Custom business expands toward its FY31 revenue target of $30 billion. In this regard, management reiterated that it expects a balanced mix of XPU and XPU Attach revenue in FY31, though it noted that either segment could grow rapidly enough to shift the mix toward 60/40 or 40/60.

    While XPU drove most of the nearly $1.5 billion Custom revenue in FY26, Svanberg expects Marvell's XPU Attach business to grow substantially through the end of the decade, leading to a more balanced mix in this business. At the Investor Day event, the organization raised its FY29 Custom target from more than $10 billion to over $12 billion, mainly driven by strength in the XPU Attach business.

    Svanberg said that another key topic in the roadshow was whether Marvell can secure enough capacity to meet its raised targets. Management said that it met with suppliers ahead of Investor Day to share its five-year goals and received commitments to support these targets. The analyst believes that Marvell's supply chain commitments give it a competitive edge over rivals as customers seek reliable partners for large-scale infrastructure buildouts.

    It has been revealed that svanberg ranks No. 91 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 58% of the time, delivering an average return of 31.8%. See Marvell Technology Statistics on TipRanks.

    #3579. 3-step method to influence people and win them over, from a Stanford expert: ‘Your voice is like a muscle’

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (687 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    3-step method to influence people and win them over, from a Stanford expert: ‘Your voice is like a muscle’

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (687 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Think back on the most memorable, inspiring speeches or presentations you've witnessed.
    • Recent findings suggest that "The human brain is designed to pick out and focus on things that are novel and fresh," notes Abrahams, a Stanford University lecturer on strategic communication and host of the "Think Fast, Talk Smart" podcast.
    • According to recent reports, indeed, successful leaders often have an uncanny ability to win over a crowd: The power of persuasion lies not just in what you actually have to say, but also in how you say it, research shows.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Think back on the most memorable, inspiring speeches or presentations you've witnessed. They probably weren't delivered in a monotone, Matt Abrahams states.

    Recent findings suggest that "The human brain is designed to pick out and focus on things that are novel and fresh," notes Abrahams, a Stanford University lecturer on strategic communication and host of the "Think Fast, Talk Smart" podcast. "So anything that stays the same, like a monotonous voice or cadence, we don't pay as much attention to.".

    According to recent reports, indeed, successful leaders often have an uncanny ability to win over a crowd: The power of persuasion lies not just in what you actually have to say, but also in how you say it, research shows. The topic has taken on new relevance this week as Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress steps into one of the most closely watched leadership roles in corporate America.

    It has been revealed that in appearances this week, including Nvidia's quarterly earnings call and an interview with CNBC's "Mad Money" host Jim Cramer, Kress has discussed the company's performance. She's also addressed employees and investors in a time of leadership upheaval, following Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang's high-profile resignation on Nov. 12.

    According to recent reports, how Kress communicates has drawn attention and, in some circles, criticism. On Wednesday, The Wall Street Journal described her public speaking style as "slow, steady, almost monotone." That doesn't necessarily make it ineffective. Her situation, however, highlights a broader challenge leaders face when they need to inform, reassure and persuade large groups of people at once.

    Generally speaking, anyone can stand a better chance at persuading others to follow them by honing an engaging speaking style, says Abrahams. Some people may be naturally expressive and engaging. For others, it's a skill that requires time and practice.

    Abrahams suggests a three-step playbook for anyone learning to speak more persuasively: "repetition, reflection and feedback.".

    Abrahams' simplest advice for making yourself a more engaging speaker: "When you're using emotive words, reflect the emotion in them." That means adding some emphasis to words like "exciting," "huge" or "challenging," and so on. If you tend to speak monotonously, leaning into obviously emotive words can help you vary your tone and inflection enough to keep your audience's attention.

    There's a catch, of course: People find inauthenticity off-putting and disingenuous, claims Abrahams. Don't alter your voice entirely, he suggests — just add some variety to your intonation and speaking volume. Learning to do so while still sounding natural takes practice, he notes.

    "Your voice is like a muscle," indicates Abrahams. "You can train it. You can grow it [and] strengthen it, just like you go to the gym to lift weights.".

    Practicing repetition starts with reading aloud from a chosen text, which Abrahams recommends so you don't have to overthink what you're saying. And the same way you might lift heavy weights to get stronger, Abrahams suggests reading overly expressive material to start getting out of your comfort zone and practice being energetic and engaging. He instructs his Stanford students to try reading Dr. Seuss books, as their playful words and bouncy rhymes can naturally make for a lively performance.

    While practicing reading out loud, record yourself to watch and listen to later, Abrahams recommends. Then, use the recording to reflect on what works and what doesn't, and incorporate your self-feedback into your next reading. You can also play the recording for a few trusted peers to get their thoughts, Abrahams claims.

    If a line reading doesn't sound natural in your voice, feels flat or even rushed, keep trying it until you're satisfied, he notes. Leaders are often asked to deliver lengthy speeches or talk for long periods in interviews and panels, so it's important to build your vocal stamina, he adds.

    "We have to calibrate ourselves," he says.

    Abrahams asks his Stanford graduate students to review their recordings in three ways, he notes:.

    "That's how you train your brain to see: 'What do I need to sound like?'" says Abrahams.

    • In a recent development, payward said late Wednesday that it's buying venture capital and asset management provider Tribe Capital Management, led by Payward's co-CEO Arjun Sethi.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Payward, the owner of crypto exchange Kraken, is pushing into private markets with its latest acquisition, underscoring a broader shift in cryptocurrencies, from trading-led growth to the buildout of financial infrastructure.

    In a recent development, payward said late Wednesday that it's buying venture capital and asset management provider Tribe Capital Management, led by Payward's co-CEO Arjun Sethi. No purchase price was disclosed.

    Tribe, where Sethi is co-founder and chairman, invests across early- and late-stage private companies and has $2.7 billion in assets under management.

    "Joining Payward gives us the opportunity to bring Tribe's investment approach to a global financial platform," Jonathan Hsu, another co-founder of Tribe Capital, remarked in a statement. "We see a strong fit between our investment approach and Payward's infrastructure, distribution, and product-building capabilities.".

    Payward didn't respond to a request for comment.

    Industry observers note that the acquisition is novel among crypto exchanges. Unlike exchange-owned venture arms such as Coinbase Ventures or Binance Labs, Payward is looking to integrate Tribe's investment and fund-management capabilities into an existing custody, trading, collateral and tokenization infrastructure to develop private-market investment products.

    Payward is trying to position itself to capture value from a broader crypto-driven transformation of financial services, not use the venture vehicle to draw more capital into the crypto ecosystem.

    According to recent reports, the acquisition is another step in the evolution in the crypto exchange business model. With cryptocurrency prices continuing to decline this year, crypto exchanges have worked to move past their reliance on trading volumes and transaction fees, focusing instead on building the infrastructure connecting digital assets with traditional finance.

    Inside India newsletter: Foreign flows helped the market recover. Now it faces the inflation test

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Hello, this is Priyanka Salve, writing to you from Singapore.
    • Welcome to the latest edition of "Inside India" — your one-stop destination for stories and developments from the world's fastest-growing large economy.
    • Industry observers note that as global portfolio managers look to diversify into non-artificial intelligence trades, India, with its strong economic growth and improved corporate earnings, is emerging as a top pick.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Hello, this is Priyanka Salve, writing to you from Singapore.

    Welcome to the latest edition of "Inside India" — your one-stop destination for stories and developments from the world's fastest-growing large economy.

    Industry observers note that as global portfolio managers look to diversify into non-artificial intelligence trades, India, with its strong economic growth and improved corporate earnings, is emerging as a top pick. But the country's inflation, which has been rising for 12 straight months, could impede inflows.

    It has been revealed that any thoughts on today's newsletter? Share them with the team.

    Foreign investors are returning to Indian equities in record numbers, but the country's accelerating inflation, which last month breached the central bank's comfort level for the first time in two years, could spoil the party.

    India's retail inflation rose to 6.09% ​in October, crossing the Reserve Bank of India's 6% upper limit, driven by surging food and transport costs.

    Experts told CNBC that businesses have already started passing on increased costs to consumers, with signs of slowing demand visible in the rural economy and expected to hurt urban consumption by early next year.

    "Rising inflation will squeeze household real incomes, while higher interest rates will weigh on investment and consumption, potentially putting pressure on corporate earnings," Alexandra Hermann Prasad, lead economist at Oxford Economics, told CNBC.

    That could "temper foreign investor enthusiasm in the near term, even if India's structural growth prospects remain attractive," she added.

    High-frequency indicators like car sales and credit card transactions softened in September while air passenger traffic declined for the fourth month in a row, Indian brokerage HDFC Securities remarked in a report on Tuesday.

    In a recent development, as per data from the Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations, released on Nov. 6, car sales fell 14.2% year on year in October. The industry body said that its "pressing concern is inventory" with dealers, which was elevated at 45 days in September and October, as against the usual range of 30 days. The inflation print "is not good," Gaura Sengupta, chief economist at India's IDFC First Bank, told CNBC, adding that inflation pressures led by supply-side shocks are spreading, and if that persists, it will affect corporate margins and household consumption.

    She expects the RBI to raise benchmark rates by 25 basis points each over the next three monetary policies, taking the terminal interest rate to 6.25% by April next year.

    The tightening of monetary policy is also likely to slow the recovery of the private investment cycle, denting India's economic outlook, experts noted.

    Recent findings suggest that so far in November, foreign investors have pumped in more than $10 billion net in Indian equities. If that sustains, it will be the highest ever foreign capital inflow in a single month.

    This would be a sharp contrast to earlier this year in March when foreign investors pulled a record $12 billion from India on worries that the energy shock from the Iran war could squeeze the economy and slow growth.

    India's growth story, however, has remained intact so far, with corporate earnings showing a sharp improvement over the last two quarters. That resilience, alongside a rotation from AI names, has drawn investors back to India, as they look to diversify into non-artificial intelligence trades.

    In a recent development, the fall in oil prices and the easing of tensions between Iran and the U.S. after the midterm poll results have also worked in India's favor, though experts warn that it is still too early to call November's rebound of foreign capital "a structural reversal.".

    "November's return of capital inflows primarily reflects lower oil prices, changing global risk sentiment following the US midterm elections, and growing concerns about the sustainability of the AI cycle, rather than a clear structural shift towards Indian assets," Hanna Luchnikava-Schorsch, head of Asia-Pacific Economics at S&P Global Market Intelligence, told CNBC.

    According to recent reports, that makes rising inflation a big worry for sustained inflows. Higher inflation could further weaken household demand, prompt monetary tightening, and slow earnings growth, making the return on Indian assets "less attractive," Luchnikava-Schorsch said.

    It has been revealed that india relies on imports to meet 85% of its crude needs and around 50% of its supplies transited through the Strait of Hormuz before the Iran war. Energy supply disruptions due to the Iran war have led to a sharp rise in inflation across several major economies in the world, including India.

    "What matters more for attracting stable, long-term capital, and for weathering short-term swings in flows, is whether India can sustain the high growth path it is on," Madhavi Bokil, executive director, credit strategy & standards at Moody's Ratings, told CNBC, adding that higher inflation is a risk to that path.

    India's inflation crosses 6% in October after rising for 12 straight monthsIndia's retail inflation rose to 6.09% ​in October, crossing the Reserve Bank of India's 6% limit for the first time under the new series, owing to surging food prices. Inflation has been on the rise for 12 straight months in the South Asian country.

    India raises export levies on diesel, aviation turbine fuel amid high inflationIndia reportedly raised export levies on diesel and jet fuel on Monday, while keeping the ‌duty on petrol exports unchanged. The increased levies on exports of key fuel items ​come on the back of rising inflation in India.

    In a recent development, nov. 19: Mahanadi Coalfields IPO opens.

    Nov.23: HSBC composite flash PMI for November.

    #3566. Amid recent banking outages, should you start carrying cash again? Top advisors weigh in

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (850 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Amid recent banking outages, should you start carrying cash again? Top advisors weigh in

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (850 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that for years, Americans have moved away from using physical U.S.
    • Sources indicate that JPMorgan Chase on Monday reported a technical issue that disrupted some consumer banking services, with ripple effects extending to several major U.S.
    • Those reports came on the heels of separate, widespread issues with Microsoft Outlook and communication systems used by air traffic control centers.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that for years, Americans have moved away from using physical U.S. currency in favor of credit, debit and digital payments. But amid the recent outages affecting some consumer banking services, experts say it's wise to revisit cash.

    Sources indicate that JPMorgan Chase on Monday reported a technical issue that disrupted some consumer banking services, with ripple effects extending to several major U.S. banks and the peer-to-peer payments network Zelle. A day later, a separate outage affected Apple, temporarily disrupting Apple Pay and iCloud, the service that keeps data available across various Apple devices.

    Those reports came on the heels of separate, widespread issues with Microsoft Outlook and communication systems used by air traffic control centers.

    Sources indicate that as technology outages expose vulnerabilities across parts of the U.S. economy, some top advisors say consumers should reconsider keeping physical money on hand.

    "This is about preparedness, not panic," stated David La Placa, CEO of Intellectus Partners in San Francisco, which ranked No. 92 on CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 list for 2026. "I think keeping some cash at home is a reasonable starting point for many households.".

    La Placa advises consumers to "build redundancy" into their financial lives.

    "Maintain access to at least a second financial institution, keep a backup credit card from a different issuer and make sure you have more than one way to access liquidity," he noted.

    It has been revealed that A client's cash management should be diversified, remarked Seth Fierston, a certified financial planner and co-president of Fierston Financial Group in West Hartford, Connecticut. The firm ranked No. 22 on CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 list.

    Having multiple accounts at brokerages or banks and various ways to move money, including Automated Clearing House, or ACH, wire, check, Venmo or Zelle, "can help mitigate technology risk," Fierston said. "One of our guiding principles is flexibility.".

    When it comes to everyday transactions, Americans are increasingly relying on digital forms of payment.

    These days, only about 46% of Americans carry cash with them always or most of the time, according to a survey of nearly 10,000 adults conducted between May and June by the Pew Research Center, a nonpartisan research group.

    Sources indicate that roughly 42% of U.S. adults stated they don't use cash for any purchases in a typical week, up from 24% in 2015, Pew found.

    Sources indicate that young adults are the least likely to carry physical currency. Among adults under 30, 51% said they go completely cashless, according to the survey.

    Industry observers note that "I recommend to my clients that they always keep three days of average cash spend on hand given the uncertainty of life in general," remarked Tim Lootens, CFP, managing director at Chilton Capital Management in Houston, which ranked No. 7 on this year's Financial Advisor 100.

    Considering the recent technical troubles, Lootens remarked consumers should keep even more cash at the ready.

    "We've had the Microsoft Outlook outage, the FAA ground shutdown and now banking disruption," he noted. "This makes me think five to seven days may be a better number.".

    According to recent reports, the right amount is as psychological as it is financial, he added. "The ability to access cash and having comfort knowing it is there when needed is so important," he said.

    Sources indicate that brian Vendig, president and chief investment officer at MJP Wealth Advisors, which ranked No. 42 on CNBC's Financial Advisor 100, also stated he recommends holding a dollar amount that corresponds with a household's discretionary living expenses. He advised having enough for at least one to two weeks, depending on their needs.

    While there is little precedent for a banking or payment system outage lasting more than a few business days, Vendig remarked, a one- to two-week cash reserve provides a "reasonable buffer" for essentials such as groceries, gas and other necessities, if electronic payments become unavailable.

    "We apply this range because it is also an emotional concern for most people, and they might want to have a little extra saved at home due to the size of their household and having a little extra 'peace of mind' guarantee," he said.

    Vendig said he recommends stashing extra cash in a secure location at home for emergency needs.

    Vendig also stated consumers should be vigilant in ensuring their electronic devices have the most recent software security patches installed.

    Criminals will try to exploit moments of uncertainty, experts say.

    "Consumers should assume they will be targeted," stated Craig Timm, senior director of anti-money laundering at ACAMS, an anti-financial crime group.

    Recent findings suggest that "[This week's] reported bank outages are likely to cause widespread confusion and fear among consumers about losing access to their money," he stated. "Criminals will try to exploit that anxiety by pushing victims to take urgent action to protect their funds or restore account access.".

    Sources indicate that as always, "stay alert, never click on links in unexpected bank messages and never share personal information such as passwords or PINs," he advised. "If you need to reach your bank, use a trusted, official channel," Timm said.

    Industry News: Anthropic IPO: Investors who flip the stock may face brokerage penalty

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Retail investors with access to Anthropic's initial public offering who sell the stock rapidly after buying could get penalized by their brokerage firm.
    • Anthropic said in an IPO prospectus that it expected to make shares available to retail investors through various brokerages, including Charles Schwab, Fidelity, Robinhood, SoFi, E-Trade and some of their respective affiliates.
    • Follow CNBC's live coverage of Anthropic's IPO and Nasdaq debut.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Retail investors with access to Anthropic's initial public offering who sell the stock rapidly after buying could get penalized by their brokerage firm.

    Anthropic said in an IPO prospectus that it expected to make shares available to retail investors through various brokerages, including Charles Schwab, Fidelity, Robinhood, SoFi, E-Trade and some of their respective affiliates.

    Follow CNBC's live coverage of Anthropic's IPO and Nasdaq debut.

    Recent findings suggest that these broker-dealers have "anti-flipping" policies meant to discourage investors who purchase IPO shares — including those of Anthropic — from dumping them quickly. Charles Schwab is the only one that doesn't have such a policy in place.

    It has been revealed that "One purpose is to discourage 'flippers' who are just buying with the hope of making a quick profit," Jay Ritter, director of The IPO Initiative at the University of Florida, remarked in an email. "Their selling could put downward pressure on the price once trading starts.".

    In a recent development, investors who run afoul of anti-flipping rules may be prohibited from accessing future IPOs, perhaps for several months or even more than a year for repeat offenders. In the worst case, the brokerage may bar them from all future IPOs.

    These policies apply only to retail investors who place an order with their brokerage firm to buy the Anthropic IPO at its offering price — something many investors don't have access to.

    In a recent development, for example, Fidelity customers are eligible to participate in the Anthropic IPO if they have at least $25,000 in certain assets, the firm said. Even then, customers are "evaluated and ranked" based on factors such as account assets to determine who can access limited shares that may be available, it said.

    Importantly, anti-flipping policies don't apply to retail investors who access shares later, once Anthropic stock starts trading on a public exchange, Ritter remarked.

    Of the retail brokerage firms listed in Anthropic's prospectus, Charles Schwab appears to be the only one without an explicit anti-flipping policy.

    "At this time, Schwab does not apply a flipping restriction to any IPOs unless required by an issuer," Margaret Farrell, a organization spokesperson, wrote in an email. "This is subject to change at Schwab's discretion.".

    She confirmed that an anti-flipping policy doesn't apply to the Anthropic IPO.

    Other firms aren't as lenient, however.

    Here's how they could penalize IPO flippers.

    E-Trade said it "prefers investors hold shares for at least 30 calendar days.".

    However, its policy doesn't lay out an explicit penalty for failing to do so.

    Selling or transferring out of an IPO within 30 days "may affect eligibility to participate in other upcoming issues in the future," according to its policy. "E*TRADE reserves the right to exclude customers from future participation.".

    Investors who are allocated Anthropic shares and sell within the first 15 calendar days from the start of trading in the secondary market won't be able to participate in future stock IPOs through Fidelity for a defined period of time, it noted:.

    "The first day clients can sell without being labeled a 'flipper' is the 16th calendar day after the IPO trades," Fidelity said.

    Robinhood's policy stipulates that selling IPO shares within 30 days of the IPO is considered flipping.

    Such investors "may be prevented from participating in IPO access for 60 days," it mentioned.

    SoFi remarked that selling an IPO position within the first 30 calendar days after trading starts "may affect your ability to participate in future IPOs on SoFi.".

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Palo Alto Networks shares rose 6% on Thursday as businesses boosted spending on cybersecurity products and investors cheered the tech giant's acquisition of a startup that pushes it into securing open-weight artificial intelligence models.
    • Industry observers note that the tech giant beat Wall Street's estimates for the fiscal first quarter.
    • It has been revealed that recent outages at Microsoft, banks and the Federal Aviation Administration have left businesses reeling.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Palo Alto Networks shares rose 6% on Thursday as businesses boosted spending on cybersecurity products and investors cheered the tech giant's acquisition of a startup that pushes it into securing open-weight artificial intelligence models.

    Industry observers note that the tech giant beat Wall Street's estimates for the fiscal first quarter. Revenue jumped 39% from a year ago and Palo Alto lifted its guidance for the year.

    It has been revealed that recent outages at Microsoft, banks and the Federal Aviation Administration have left businesses reeling. While U.S. officials haven't detected any malicious activity, the disruptions raise concerns over aging equipment and infrastructure. Many businesses are scrambling to patch vulnerabilities at a faster clip than ever before to keep pace with the growing risks of AI-powered cyberattacks.

    Those fears have led more businesses to consolidate platforms, which is fueling growth in areas like firewall and AI security, Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora told CNBC's "Mad Money" on Wednesday.

    "They're going to have to make sure they get the best players in the market to come support them because this is no longer child's play," Arora mentioned.

    According to recent reports, alongside earnings, Palo Alto announced a $4.5 billion deal to buy Applied Compute, a startup that helps train customized open-weight models. It's one of several recent deals in Arora's aggressive acquisition spree and marks a significant shift beyond cybersecurity.

    "Rather than being one player out of 10 in the industry serving compute, we want to be the one player with Palo Alto that delivers secure compute and security capability," Arora told CNBC.

    Palo Alto expects the deal to add more than $1 billion in annual recurring revenue to its next-generation security business by the 2029 fiscal year.

    Analysts at Bank of America touted the deal as a "bold move" to expand beyond securing AI into training open-weight models, allowing Palo Alto to lead the next phase of the AI revolution.

    This "appears consistent with PANW's 'long-game' - become indispensable beyond cyber into multidisciplinary IT domains across AI-value-chain," wrote analysts at Citigroup.

    WATCH: Palo Alto Networks shares surge.

    #3555. Amazon app warns Latest York of higher costs if Mamdani delivery law passes

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (622 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Amazon app warns Latest York of higher costs if Mamdani delivery law passes

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (622 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Amazon is taking its fight against a Fresh York City delivery bill, which has been backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, to its shopping website and app.
    • Some users who open the firm's shopping app or website report being served with pop-ups and banners warning that the Upcoming York City Council "could add up to $5 per order" if it passes Intro 518, or the Delivery Protection Act.
    • It has been revealed that the bill would require Amazon to employ its army of third-party delivery companies directly, disrupting the contractor model it has relied on since 2018.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Amazon is taking its fight against a Fresh York City delivery bill, which has been backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, to its shopping website and app.

    Some users who open the firm's shopping app or website report being served with pop-ups and banners warning that the Upcoming York City Council "could add up to $5 per order" if it passes Intro 518, or the Delivery Protection Act.

    It has been revealed that the bill would require Amazon to employ its army of third-party delivery companies directly, disrupting the contractor model it has relied on since 2018. Amazon uses a network of thousands of small companies, which often work solely for Amazon, to handle the last-mile portion of shipments, in an effort to speed up deliveries and control more of its logistics operations.

    Recent findings suggest that "If this legislation passes, we'd no longer be able to work with them, and we'd be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city," Amazon's in-app message states. "That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in Fresh York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.".

    The proposed legislation was introduced in February and is awaiting review by City Council Speaker Julie Menin.

    Amazon also posted a statement on its firm website where it often publishes its policy positions. But rarely has the company used its valuable e-commerce site and app real estate to push its perspectives. Other tech companies including Uber and Lyft have similarly used their apps to advocate for or against legislation in the past.

    Amazon's pop-up notices and a stationary banner on its store homepage direct owners to a form where they can "contact your council member to oppose Intro 518.".

    According to Amazon, 20,000 customers sent emails to city council members in the first six hours that the pop-up appeared.

    Menin told CNBC in a statement that Amazon's claim it will need to raise prices due to the proposed legislation "defies logic.".

    Sources indicate that "We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs," Menin said. "If Amazon thinks this deceptive campaign will effectively threaten New Yorkers and intimidate this City Council, they are dead wrong.".

    Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in a statement that the company put up the notices to be "transparent with our customers" about what the bill "would cause them if it passes as written.".

    "If customers are concerned, one of the most impactful things they can do is contact their City Council member and ask them to oppose this bill," Nantel noted.

    The Delivery Protection Act has received a swell of support from labor groups, including the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, which has sought to unionize Amazon delivery and warehouse workers.

    Mamdani endorsed the bill in August, saying Amazon's subcontractor model "leaves workers vulnerable and corporations free to avoid accountability for reckless conditions on city streets." He's argued the bill would lead to safer working conditions for drivers, and allow the city to "regulate last-mile operations.".

    Amazon disputed Mamdani's claims, saying the bill would put Delivery Service Partner jobs "at risk without improving safety." It also argued that other businesses and governments use contractors in their operations, and mentioned the DSP model has allowed it to meet growing customer demand.

    In a recent development, "It works because local entrepreneurs — people rooted in their communities — deliver a better experience," Amazon mentioned. "They invest in their teams, their routes, and their neighborhoods. That's not a liability play.".

    Amazon has lobbied heavily against the bill, while logistics and business groups have introduced local advertising campaigns, and warned they may sue the city if the bill passes.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that global stock markets remain volatile amid persistent geopolitical tensions and concerns about the sustainability of AI trade.
    • Tracking recommendations from top Wall Street analysts can help investors pick attractive stocks, as these experts assess a company's ability to pay dividends consistently.
    • Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that global stock markets remain volatile amid persistent geopolitical tensions and concerns about the sustainability of AI trade. Given this backdrop, investors seeking steady income can add dividend-paying stocks to their portfolios.

    Tracking recommendations from top Wall Street analysts can help investors pick attractive stocks, as these experts assess a company's ability to pay dividends consistently.

    Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

    Integrated oil and gas giant Chevron (CVX) is a dividend king. The organization has increased its dividend for 39 consecutive years. At a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share (annualized dividend of $7.12 per share), CVX offers a yield of 3.14%. Chevron will announce its third-quarter results on October 30.

    Sources indicate that in an earnings preview note on U.S. oil majors, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on Chevron with a price target of $241. The analyst is focused on the company's international growth prospects across Latin America, the Middle East, West Africa, and the Eastern Mediterranean.

    Specifically, Mehta highlighted management's commentary on solid execution in Venezuela, with gross production expected to more than double to nearly 600 kbd (kilo barrels per day) by 2031 via three joint ventures. He also noted a recent oil and gas condensate discovery in offshore Angola and is awaiting commercial updates on the West Qurna 2 and Nasiriyah projects in Iraq.

    Furthermore, Mehta expects CVX to report improved productivity and capital efficiency across domestic shale assets. He expects the improvement mainly in the Permian Basin, where Chevron projects advanced chemical treatments to drive about a 10% recovery uplift in newly introduced wells and bring down capital spend per barrel by about 25% year-over-year. Overall, Mehta expects Chevron to report Q3 2026 EPS of $4.95, above the consensus of $4.89.

    According to recent reports, "While unfavorable timing effects and volatile commodity prices may present quarterly earnings headwinds, we highlight healthy U.S. refining margins and strong asset utilization as partial offsets," noted Mehta.

    Mehta ranks No. 381 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of 12%. See Chevron KPIs on TipRanks.

    Kinetik Holdings (KNTK) is a fully integrated, pure-play, midstream organization operating in the Delaware Basin. Earlier this month, the company declared a dividend of $0.81 per share, payable on October 30, 2026. With an annualized dividend of $3.24 per share, KNTK offers a yield of 5.82%. Kinetik will announce its Q3 earnings on November 4, with a conference call scheduled the next day.

    Ahead of Q3 2026 earnings, Goldman Sachs analyst John Mackay reiterated a buy rating on Kinetik stock and slightly raised his price target to $58 from $57. He expects the company to report Q3 2026 EBITDA of $279 million, higher than the Street's expectation of $270 million but lower than the second quarter's EBITDA of $281 million.

    It has been revealed that the 5-star analyst expects Kinetik's Q3 performance to gain from higher gas volumes after notable curtailments in the second quarter. Mackay also expects the quarter to benefit from higher production and steady commodity margins, even though some lower-margin contracts and weaker Waha spread marketing gains could weigh on results.

    Overall, Mackay increased his Q3 2026 estimates to reflect higher volumes, driven by rapid Permian egress pipeline commissioning, stronger throughput at Kings Landing I, and higher M2M commodity prices, offset by increased costs.

    "As natural gas takeaway constraints ease across the Permian, investor focus centers on KNTK's YE26 volume trajectory and durability of its multi-year growth," noted Mackay.

    Mackay ranks No. 569 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 16.9%. See Kinetik's Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

    Moving to Crescent Energy (CRGY), an exploration and production company with activities focused in the Eagle Ford, Permian, and Uinta Basins. With a quarterly dividend of $0.12 per share (annualized dividend of $0.48 per share), CRGY's dividend yield stands at 3.56%. Earlier this month, Crescent announced an agreement to acquire Eagle Ford assets from Devon Energy (DVN).

    According to recent reports, heading into Q3 earnings on Nov. 2, Evercore analyst Stephen Richardson reiterated a buy rating on Crescent stock and slightly lowered the price target to $17 from $18, citing dilution from new shares.

    "CRGY's recent acquisition of DVN's Eagle Ford assets marks a strategic, growth-oriented move, potentially enhancing cash flow performance," said Richardson.

    In a recent development, the 5-star analyst noted that the acquisition of the Eagle Ford assets at a net purchase price of $3.85 billion will add about 68 MBoe/d of net production and over 600 net Tier 1 locations. Richardson added that a solid track record of synergies from past deals in the Eagle Ford region increases confidence about Crescent achieving efficiencies with this deal.

    Additionally, Richardson noted that the financial implications of the acquisition seem impressive, with a projected increase in cash flow per share of about 9% for 2027 to 2029.

    The analyst believes that Crescent is not just expanding its business through acquisitions but positioning itself as a more durable manufacturer, regardless of market conditions.

    Richardson ranks No. 478 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.2%. See Crescent Energy Statistics on TipRanks.

    #3548. Trump bought Nvidia, Palantir, SpaceX in September as federal deals, White House ties grew

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (905 w)
    📖 Baca
    Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Trump bought Nvidia, Palantir, SpaceX in September as federal deals, White House ties grew

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (905 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • President Donald Trump's investment accounts bought shares of Nvidia, Palantir and Elon Musk's SpaceX in September, around the time the companies secured major federal contracts and their executives met with the president, according to a newly released financial disclosure.
    • The 25-page filing demonstrates 751 purchases and sales totaling between roughly $40.9 million and $148.1 million, according to a CNBC analysis.
    • Among the transactions were Palantir purchases before the company received two federal contracts worth $42.5 million combined, according to contracting records, SpaceX investments shortly before and after a $946 million NASA contract expansion, and Nvidia trades as its then-CEO, Jensen Huang, cultivated a close relationship with Trump.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    President Donald Trump's investment accounts bought shares of Nvidia, Palantir and Elon Musk's SpaceX in September, around the time the companies secured major federal contracts and their executives met with the president, according to a newly released financial disclosure.

    The 25-page filing demonstrates 751 purchases and sales totaling between roughly $40.9 million and $148.1 million, according to a CNBC analysis. Purchases accounted for at least $29.2 million and sales at least $11.7 million. The filing reports transactions in broad dollar ranges, leaving the exact amounts and value of Trump's holdings unclear.

    Among the transactions were Palantir purchases before the company received two federal contracts worth $42.5 million combined, according to contracting records, SpaceX investments shortly before and after a $946 million NASA contract expansion, and Nvidia trades as its then-CEO, Jensen Huang, cultivated a close relationship with Trump.

    In a recent development, the trades underscore a striking feature of Trump's presidency: His personal fortune remains invested in companies whose fortunes his administration can shape. His accounts reported more than 21,000 trades in 2025, compared with roughly 500 during his entire first term. Recent presidents have generally divested individual stocks or used blind trusts to avoid potential conflicts.

    The White House has told CNBC previously Trump and his family have no control over the trades, which outside financial managers handle independently. The Trump Organization says the arrangement is designed to avoid even the appearance of a conflict. There is no evidence Trump directed the transactions or that his managers knew government decisions in advance.

    According to recent reports, white House spokesman Davis Ingle said that Trump's portfolio is independently managed and that neither the president nor his family has any input on trades. "All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers," Ingle told CNBC.

    The Trump Organization did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

    Industry observers note that the timing was particularly notable at Palantir, the artificial intelligence software maker whose technology is used by U.S. military, intelligence and civilian agencies.

    Trump's accounts bought between $15,001 and $50,000 in Palantir shares on Sept. 2, followed by another purchase of between $1,001 and $15,000 on Sept. 9.

    A week later, the Department of Housing and Urban Development awarded Palantir a contract with $10.4 million in initial obligations for AI-powered grant oversight and fraud detection.

    It has been revealed that on Sept. 29, the Department of Homeland Security awarded Palantir another $32.1 million software contract, bringing the two awards to roughly $42.5 million. That same day, CEO Alex Karp joined Trump, Musk, Huang and other technology executives at the White House for a meeting on artificial intelligence.

    Trump's accounts also bought shares and debt in SpaceX in the weeks surrounding a major NASA contract award.

    On Sept. 1, the accounts purchased between $100,001 and $250,000 in SpaceX debt carrying a 5.35% interest rate. Eight days later, they bought between $1,001 and $15,000 in shares of the major NASA and Pentagon contractor.

    Sources indicate that on Sept. 18, NASA revealed a $946 million expansion of its SpaceX contract, adding three astronaut missions to the International Space Station and bringing the agreement's total value to $5.92 billion. The agency had signaled intends for additional missions in May.

    Six days after the announcement, Trump's accounts bought another $15,001 to $50,000 in SpaceX shares on the same day Musk attended Trump's White House state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping. The filing does not show whether the purchase came before or after the dinner.

    The trades followed an even larger SpaceX investment in August, when Trump's accounts bought between $1 million and $5 million in the company's debt just two days before he signed a policy aimed at expanding commercial space transportation.

    Trump's accounts also continued buying Nvidia shares as Huang drew closer to the president — a relationship now under congressional scrutiny over Huang's ties to a woman suspected of spying for China.

    The September filing shows four Nvidia purchases totaling between $152,004 and $380,000, including two on Sept. 2 worth as much as $350,000 combined.

    In a recent development, the accounts also sold between $1,001 and $15,000 in Nvidia shares on Sept. 24, the day Huang also attended the state dinner with Xi.

    The trades bring Trump's Nvidia transactions to at least 108 since his return to office in 2025, worth between $27.2 million and $97.9 million, extending a CNBC analysis published Monday.

    The relationship between the president and Nvidia's then-CEO has drawn fresh scrutiny after The New York Times reported that intelligence officials warned Trump about Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Trump has denied being briefed. Huang resigned Nov. 12 following revelations about his personal relationships.

    In a recent development, the September filing also shows substantial trading beyond the three companies. The largest reported transaction was a Sept. 23 purchase of between $5 million and $25 million in Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF shares.

    That same day, Trump's accounts sold between $1 million and $5 million each in Comcast, McDonald's, Home Depot and Fidelity National Information Services, along with between $500,001 and $1 million each in Nike and Constellation Brands.

    Industry observers note that on the buy side, Trump's accounts purchased between $250,001 and $500,000 in TJX shares on each of two consecutive days, Sept. 15 and 16. They also bought between $117,004 and $330,000 in Tesla shares across four transactions, along with smaller investments in CoreWeave, Intel, Microsoft and Apple.
